body: In a hall with a low ceiling and stacking chairs and a tea urn at the back, a room full of people is singing a hymn at a funeral. The tune came off a ship. The words are in a language that the schools some of their grandparents were sent to punished children for speaking. A man near the front is holding the printed sheet and not looking at it, because he has known it since he was small. Two rows back a woman sings the harmony part her aunt used to sing and gets it slightly wrong in the same place. Nobody in the hall finds any of this complicated. They are burying somebody.

It is complicated everywhere except in that room. Outside it, the same three facts — the tune, the language, the schools — are the beginning of an argument that has been running for a long time and that most Christian broadcasting will not go anywhere near.
It has to be gone near, because for a great many Native and Indigenous listeners it is the first question and not the last one. The faith did not arrive here neutrally. It came bundled.

That word is worth taking literally. A message travels in the hands of the people carrying it, and those hands are never empty of anything else. What arrived alongside the gospel in a great many places was land changing owners, a legal apparatus that made it stick, schools children were removed to, languages forbidden in the mouths of the young, and the settled confidence that becoming Christian meant ceasing to be what you had been. Some of those people were sincere. It made no practical difference at the receiving end whether they were, and it makes none now to the families still counting the cost.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations in 29 languages, 46 of them on air. Some frequencies this argument bears on are assigned and still in build: HM 330.90, West Africa Inspire in Yorùbá, and HM 331.50, Ethiopia Inspire in Amharic, are held and silent. HM 312.10, Island Hallelujah, is on air now.

Building them in that order costs money and time, and the cheaper option is always available: take the existing catalogue, dub it, and call the result a station for those people. It is not done that way here. A frequency is held empty until somebody who belongs to the language is doing the programming, because a translated worship hour tells a listener, in a way no disclaimer can undo, that their language is a delivery format for somebody else’s. The message was carried by people who also carried a great deal else. Sorting one from the other is the work of several generations, and it is not optional.

Two responses to that history are common, and both are evasions. The first says it was regrettable, it was long ago, and we should all move forward — which sounds generous and quietly assigns the moving to the injured party, who did not raise the subject. The second concludes that a message is inseparable from the people who delivered it, and that the whole thing should be set down where they left it. That one has more dignity. It is also the outcome the worst of those men would have chosen, had they been asked.

The band is arranged so that the international frequencies are hosted rather than dubbed, and grouped where a listener can find them by feel. That is structural, not a courtesy. It means the person choosing the songs and deciding what a Sunday sounds like is inside the language rather than translating into it, and it means a station carries the local instruments and the local harmony without anybody having to approve them. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about the dial without looking, which is what a real band teaches.
The harder position than either evasion is to hold both halves of the sentence at once, and to keep holding them.

Be fair to the second response first, because the people who hold it have generally paid for the right to. It is not petulance. It is the reasonable observation that a book quoted at your grandmother while her language was being taken off her is compromised as evidence, and that the burden of proof is not on her. But look at what it concedes. It hands the men who did the damage permanent ownership of the text they were misusing. And it gives away the one document in which a king is taken apart for stealing one man’s vineyard, in which the prophets spend their working lives on people who join field to field until there is no room for anybody else, and in which the central figure was born under an occupying power and executed by it.
The strongest available indictment of what happened comes from inside the book, not from outside it.

A woman in her twenties is sitting in a parked truck outside her grandmother’s house with the engine off and her phone propped under the windscreen, recording. Her grandmother is in the passenger seat with her coat still done up because it is cold, singing a verse she has not sung in front of anybody for years. She gets three lines in, stops, and says the fourth in English, because that is how it was taught to her and how it comes. Then she says a word to herself twice, quietly, starts the verse again from the top and gets all four. The recording is nine minutes long and most of it is the two of them not saying anything.

A language was being handed forward one verse at a time by somebody taught to be ashamed of it, and the shame was the part that had to be got past first. That is the sorting, and that is what it looks like being done.

It has to be said plainly that none of this repairs anything. A station returns no land. It does not reopen a file, find a grave, or give a family back the years in which nobody spoke to each other about any of it. Worship in the language is not compensation and it would be obscene to offer it as any. Some people will hear all of the above and decline, and they are not being unreasonable, and nothing in this article is owed a yes.

But consider what the intended outcome was. The assimilation policies of that era were not shy about their aim, which was that the languages would not continue. So a woman in a truck singing four lines of one into a phone for her granddaughter is not a consolation prize. It is the specific thing that was meant not to survive, surviving, and being spent on the one purpose those men would have claimed to want. The tune off the ship stays. The language comes back. Nobody has to choose.

So both halves of that sentence are true and both have to be said in one breath. It arrived here in the wrong hands, at a cost still being paid in families that can name it. And it is still the gospel — not despite the people who misused it but in judgement on them, because the standard they failed is the one printed in the book they were carrying. Holding both is heavier than picking one. It is also the only position that leaves anything standing.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it is worth knowing they are there before you turn it. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. No menu, no queue, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 312.10 — Island Hallelujah. It is on air, and it is the frequency on this dial that already does what the argument above is asking for. It is praise carried in the language, the harmony and the instruments of a place with its own version of this history, which did not need the question settled in a magazine before it started singing. Nothing on it is a translation. It is not an apology set to music either, which matters, because an apology would put the people who did the damage back at the centre of it. It is worship that belongs to somebody, going out at a number that is theirs.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next one gets built and in which language.

So take this as an invitation and not a settlement, because a settlement is not on offer and would be an insult if it were. Put HM 312.10 on this week while you are doing something else and let it run. Listen to what a language sounds like when nobody is translating it and nobody is asking it to explain itself. Then, if somebody in your family still has four lines of something, go and sit in the car with them and let them sing it. It is nine minutes. It is most of the work.
